div.head: II Ew 5.2
div.ab: Gif hine hwa feormige syððan, bete swa seo domboc sæcge, ⁊ se scyle ðe flyman feormige, gif hit sy herinne; gif hit sy east inne, gif hit sy norð inne, bete be ðam þe þa friðgehwritu sæcgan.
Gyf hine hwa feormige syððan, bete swa seo domboc secge, ⁊ se scyle ðe flyman feormie, gyf hit sy herinne; gif hit sy east inne, gif hit sy norð inne, bete be ðam ðe ða friðgewritu secgan.

Si quis eum deinceps firmabit, emendet sicut liber iudiciorum docet, ac debet qui flyman (id est forisbannitum) confirmabit, si sit hic intus; si sit east intro, si sit norđ intus, emendet sicut scripta pacis continent.
Gif hine hwa feormige syððan, bete swa seo domboc sæcge, ⁊ se scyle ðe flyman feormige, gif hit sy herinne; gif hit sy east inne, gif hit sy norð inne, bete be ðam þe þa friðgewritu sæcgan.

Wenn ihn einer nachher beherbergt, büsse er so, wie das Gesetzbuch besagt, und [zwar, wie] der, welcher einen Geächteten beherbergt, [büssen] muss, falls es hier im [Englischen] Innenlande geschieht; wenn es im Ost[anglischen Lande] geschieht, [oder] wenn es im Nord[humbrischen Lande] geschieht, büsse er gemäss dem, was die Friedensartikel [mit den Nordleuten vereinbart] besagen.

If anyone afterwards harbours him, let him pay compensation as the law-book says, and [namely as] he who harbours an outlaw must [pay], if it happens here in the [English] inland; if it happens in the East[-Anglian land], [or] if it happens in the North[umbrian land], let him pay according to what the peace-articles [agreed with the Northmen] say.

If anyone subsequently harbours him, he shall pay such compensation as the written laws declare of him who harbours a fugitive, if the offence is committed in our own kingdom. If the offence is committed in the eastern or northern kingdoms, compensation shall be paid in accordance with the provisions of the treaties.

Nicht ‘in this part of the country’, sondern Wessex weiteren Sinnes mit Mercien und Kent
Not ‘in this part of the country’, but Wessex in the wider sense, including Mercia and Kent
Gleich þær on lande EGu 12. Als Präposition und Adverb steht in und inne bisweilen dem Orte nach; Toller 589b III. 595a. Vgl. Gl Ostanglien 5a; Northumbrien 1
Equivalent to þær on lande EGu 12. As preposition and adverb, in and inne sometimes follow the place-name; Toller 589b III. 595a. Cf. Gl Ostanglien 5a; Northumbrien 1

Nicht ‘Schriften’; vielleicht hat der Pl., wie oft litterae übersetzend, singularische Bed. — Dieser Vertrag mit einer Satzung über Begünstigung ist verloren. Eine darüber wird aufgenommen in II Atr 6, 2. In III 13 (ebd. 8b) steht ein Reinigungsbeweis von Anklage auf Begünstigung aus Denalagu, von Westsächs. Recht abweichend.—Hiermit wird Northumbrien zuerst in Englischer Gesetzgebung erwähnt, aber noch nicht (wie IV Eg 2, 1) von ihr beeinflusst; vielmehr richtet sich dieses Northumbrische Recht noch nach einem internationalen Vertrage

Not ‘writings’; perhaps the pl., as often when translating litterae, has a singular meaning. — This treaty, with its enactment on harbouring, is lost. One on this subject is included in II Atr 6, 2. In III 13 (ibid. 8b) there is a proof of clearance from a charge of harbouring, from the Danelaw, differing from West Saxon law. — This is the first mention of Northumbria in English legislation, though Northumbria is not yet influenced by it (as it is in IV Eg 2, 1); rather, this Northumbrian law is still governed by an international treaty
Cf. Ine, cap. 30, etc. (see Index, s.v. ‘fugitive’).

Edward’s dominions at his accession comprised Wessex, together with Kent, etc. and English Mercia (i.e. the south-western half of the Midlands). Before his death he had carried his frontier as far as Nottingham and Manchester.

i.e. East Anglia and Northumbria. The former kingdom was conquered by Edward after the battle of Tempsford, in which the East Anglian king was killed. The date is uncertain; the Saxon Chronicle (A) gives it under the annal 921, but the dates of this text are, in general, three or four years in advance of those of B and C.

These treaties are now lost, the Laws of Edward and Guthrum containing no provisions of this kind. This passage seems to me (as against Liebermann’s view) to point to a date before the conquest of the East Anglian kingdom, since this kingdom is treated on a par with the Northumbrian kingdom which was still in existence at Edward’s death, though it had already recognised his supremacy.
